messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: feature request: pedantic mode
parts:
Hi!

Would it be possible to issue a warning if a defined parameter has no prior set?

I just discovered that I extended my model and simply forgot to set a prior on some parameters which caused some sampling issues. An option somewhere making stan a bit noisy if no priors are used would be great. I definitely prefer to go with weakly informative priors and would like to be reminded of that…

Best,

--
Sebastian Weber

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request: pedantic mode
parts:
It's not so easy to figure that out in Stan because
it's not a graphical model language that can be
inspected structurally. Some models have implicit
priors due to constraints and others can have priors
implemented by direct manipulation of lp__. Also,
the dynamic nature of our indexing makes the calculation
difficult.

What we have thought about doing is issuing a warning
if not every parameter showed up on the left-hand side
of a ~ in the model. That I can probably calculate
pretty easily from the syntax tree for the model itself.

This wouldn't catch errors like:

for (n in 2:N)
sigma[n] ~ cauchy(0,5);

where you don't have a prior for sigma[1]. I could even
figure out how to turn off false positives for parameters
with finite support (upper and lower bounded, simplex, correlation
matrix), which get implicit uniform priors if no other priors
are provided.

We could issue warnings if a variable showed up twice,
but this would issue a false positive in the correct
variant of the above that included a sampling statement
for sigma[1],

sigma[1] ~ cauchy(0,5);

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request: pedantic mode
parts:
On 2/17/13 11:36 AM, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
> Hmm, I understand its difficult, but something in this direction would be very helpful. I would be very interested to know if an improper prior is used in my model, because I did not specify a sampling statement. I simplify prefer to go with proper priors (and hence even a half-positive prior should pop up in these warnings). Of course, others may disagree such that this has to be optional after all.

I agree as far as providing warnings goes.
Unlike with error messages, it's only polite to provide
flags to control the verbosity of warnings.

Because we only need the probability up to a proportion,
we're OK with unnormalized priors. So if you have:

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
...
}
model {
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
}

the model is technically not normalized correctly. You really need to
write the half-Cauchy properly via truncation:

sigma ~ cauchy(0,5) T[0,];

This isn't necessary in Stan for sampling because the Cauchy's
parameters (0 and 5 here) are fixed.

Figuring out better warnings in case 0 or 5 were not
fixed is tricky as it involves reasoning about constraints
and support of distributions. It's not that this information
isn't available, but that it can involve a lot of
interpretation to understand it. For instance, the lower
bound can be one expression and the truncation another expression
and they'd need to be evaluated relative to parameters or
data.

> BTW, stan is really stunningï¿½ if one could hat differential equation support there would be no more need for any other software when it comes to parameter inference...

Thanks.

What do you mean by diff eq support? We've been
thinking about adding implicitly defined functions with
iterative solvers.

Well, there are still scalability issues. And models
with crazy posterior geometries. We're addressing both
of these issues in our research, but they won't hit
Stan right away.

We are going to be adding some max a posteriori inference,
which will basically just run an optimizer instead of
an HMC/NUTS sampler.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request: pedantic mode
parts: Hi!

> I agree as far as providing warnings goes.
> Unlike with error messages, it's only polite to provide
> flags to control the verbosity of warnings.
>

That's what I meant - just warnings which can even be turned of. How people chose priors or do not, well that anyone has to decide for himself or just trust the defaults which is dangerous in Bayesian world in my opinion.

>

> What do you mean by diff eq support? We've been
> thinking about adding implicitly defined functions with
> iterative solvers.

I mean by differential equations that it is possible to write down

dy/dt = k * y

And this would give me the parameter of the solution to y=y0 * exp(k *t). In the current Stan world I could write down my functions as transformations of the parameters, but only if I have an integrated form of my differential equation system available, which is not always the case

implicitly defined functions could solve the problem here maybe. To my understanding, one should be able to get numerically the likelihood contribution given the parameter which are being sampled. I.e. an ode solver would have to obtain in each iteration the numerical solution and summarize everything into a LL contribution. But I thought then the whole beauty of HMC to make use of partial derivates simply breaks down, because the integration can only be performed numerically by these *soda Fortran routines.

>
> Well, there are still scalability issues. And models
> with crazy posterior geometries. We're addressing both
> of these issues in our research, but they won't hit
> Stan right away.

Well, for me I do not see any point any more in sticking to jags or any other bugs variant, which I used before Stan - so Stan is from my perspective far more usable than anything out there (given my personal applications...). Only WinBugs which has PkBUGS included has differential equation support which is a must in my research.

>
> We are going to be adding some max a posteriori inference,
> which will basically just run an optimizer instead of
> an HMC/NUTS sampler.

Is that something like inla?

Sebastian

We've been thinking about doing something like
this. We'd have to write our own ODE solver (we
already have one for the Hamiltonian simulations)
from which we could take gradients. There are
various ways described for doing this in the
auto-diff literature.

I'm afraid to say it's not near the top of our
priority list, but we have a colleague in Paris who
might help us push it up the list.

- Bob
